doc.title: Billy Bauer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 22, 1998

title: Father the printer; ukulele, mandolin and the Weymann banjo
summary: His father, a printer who nearly made Broadway, gave him a ukulele when he broke his leg at nine; the stage-fright debut led to a mandolin and a banjo he still owns.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: That’s right. What did your father do for a living?

He was a printer. He was really a song and dance man like I said, and he made, there was an audition — I wasn’t born about this time but he’d tell me that the audition was Ned Wayburn “School Days.” It got to be a big Broadway show. And they went up to Ossining, New York to break it in. And he made it as one of the guys in the cast, not the star. And as he went up to Ossining, which isn’t far from the Bronx, and his father told him if he could quit for show business was out. My grandfather, he thought that that was bad. So he says if you don’t, you ain’t got no place there, get out on your own. So my father got afraid, and come back and my grandfather was a printer, he became a printer. And he tried to do, later he tried to do the same thing with me. You know like because I started when I was nine. I broke my leg, my father bought me a ukulele while the girl pushed me around in a baby carriage, they didn’t have no big things, they just got an old baby carriage. And I was laid up for a couple of months with this big cast, you know you had a cast on your leg. You mind me telling you all this?
No I want to hear this.

So to keep me busy, he gave me a ukulele. At that time Harold Teen and Cliff Edwards, Ukulele Ike. And they’d play “five foot two, eyes of blue, koochie, koochie—” and that kind of thing. And for some reason I learned a couple of chords, and by the time my leg was better at the end of the summer, me and my cousin went on to summer school, the two ukuleles, we’d practice all day, and we got out there. Well I have this in my book you know. And you mind me telling you?

They pushed us, it was our act. We got out there and we both froze. You know well we were never on the — I was never on the stage and the damn stage, the people were — so I ran up the stairs and I ran right into a little girl’s dressing room. So they pushed me back on to the stage. By the time I got back my cousin was gone, he must have took off. So I don’t know what I did. I know I went — so they gave us ice cream, that was the end. But

that was the first time I was ever in front of an audience you know. And from then, then he got me a mandolin for a little while. I didn’t like it. It isn’t that I didn’t like it, I didn’t know what to do with it. Then he got me a banjo. And I’ve still got the banjo.
Yeah that he bought. It was about a hundred dollars, so it was a Weymann banjo, and it’s a great banjo, but I’ve used it all these years.
And a hundred dollars at that time was significant.
It was a lot, yeah. And he thought because I could do these things.
